**Reading time:** about 4 minutes. **Goal:** discover Plato's family background while distinguishing plausible history from inherited stories.

Plato was probably born around **428/427 BC**, into a well-connected Athenian family. His exact birthplace is uncertain in the ancient traditions: Athens and Aegina are both mentioned. His family's standing helps explain why questions of civic life and political responsibility were close to his world, but it cannot by itself explain the philosophy he would later write.

Ancient accounts name his father **Ariston** and his mother **Perictione**. They also report striking claims about their ancestry. Ariston's family was said to descend from **Codrus**, the legendary Athenian king, while Perictione's was connected with **Solon**, the lawgiver associated with Athens' earlier political reforms. Such traditions reveal how families presented their prestige; they are not the same as a securely documented family tree.

## Brothers, sister and relatives

Plato's brothers **Glaucon** and **Adeimantus** appear as important interlocutors in the *Republic*. In Book II, they press Socrates to explain why justice is worth choosing for its own sake, even when injustice may appear more profitable. Their questions shape the discussion, but we should not mistake the literary dialogue for a transcript of family conversations.

Plato also had a sister, **Potone**. Her son **Speusippus** later succeeded Plato as head of the Academy. Ancient testimony gives us a glimpse of a family whose connections continued into the history of philosophy; it does not prove that every member shared the same intellectual ambitions.

Another relative, **Charmides**, appears as a character in the dialogue bearing his name. Family links also connected Plato to **Critias**, a prominent figure among the Thirty who governed Athens after its defeat in 404 BC. Their political histories were not all alike, and their appearance in the dialogues should not be read as an endorsement of their conduct.

## Was his name really Plato?

A later account preserved by **Diogenes Laertius** says that Plato was originally called *Aristocles* and received the name *Platon*—related to the Greek word for “broad”—as a nickname. Different explanations were offered, including his build, forehead and style.

The story is memorable, but it is **not certain**. We cannot use it to establish details of Plato's athletic training or personality. It is a good example of how biography can gradually gather anecdotes around a celebrated figure.

## A stepfather with political connections

After Ariston's death, Perictione married **Pyrilampes**, an Athenian associated with Pericles' political circle. In the *Charmides* (158a), he is recalled as a distinguished envoy who travelled in Asia. Perictione and Pyrilampes had a son, **Antiphon**, mentioned as Plato's half-brother in the *Parmenides* (126a–b).

These connections placed Plato's household within a world attentive to public affairs. We do not, however, know the precise conversations he heard as a child or the extent of his early involvement in politics.

## Expectations and political choices

For a young man of Plato's status, education and public service were familiar expectations. Yet his adult relationship to Athenian politics was not simply inherited from his family. His dialogues question the meaning of leadership, the value of knowledge in government and the responsibilities of citizens.

The **Seventh Letter**, whose authenticity remains disputed, offers a retrospective account of political disappointment and the death of Socrates. It can illuminate the way Plato's political vocation was later understood, but it cannot be used without qualification as a direct autobiography.

What matters most is the distinction between **background and explanation**. Plato grew up among powerful families and conflicting political traditions. Those circumstances help us understand the questions available to him; they do not predetermine the answers of his philosophy.

## Family connections

- **Ariston** — father; legendary descent from Codrus was claimed by later accounts.
- **Perictione** — mother; connected by tradition to Solon's family.
- **Glaucon and Adeimantus** — brothers; speakers in the *Republic*.
- **Potone** — sister; mother of Speusippus.
- **Pyrilampes** — stepfather, associated with Pericles.
- **Antiphon** — half-brother, mentioned in the *Parmenides*.

## Key terms

- **Genos** (γένος) — family descent or lineage.
- **Oikos** (οἶκος) — household and its members, property and obligations.
- **Dēmos** (δῆμος) — the people or citizen body, depending on context.
- **Aristokratia** (ἀριστοκρατία) — literally rule by the best; not simply a synonym for inherited wealth.

## Learn more

- *Republic* II, 357a–368c — Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates about justice.
- *Charmides* 155a–158b — family connections and Pyrilampes.
- *Parmenides* 126a–b — Antiphon.
- *Seventh Letter* 324b–326b — an account of political hopes and disappointments, **if authentic**.

## Sources and historical orientation

- Diogenes Laertius, *Lives of Eminent Philosophers* III 1–6 (late testimony on genealogy and the name).
- Plato, *Republic* II 357a–368c; *Charmides* 155a–158b; *Parmenides* 126a–b (dramatic and familial references).
- *Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, “Plato,” biography; *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, “Plato” (modern discussions of biographical uncertainty).
- Cambridge University Press, *Plato's Charmides*, commentary on 155a and 158a (qualifies the Solon connection and explains Pyrilampes' political milieu).
